ideation · 2

Candidate Law ideation · earlier check spanned 37 channels
strong Reproduced The same relationship showed up on independent channels. Much harder to explain as coincidence — still not a demonstrated cause. held 85% of 33 measurements 6 channels
A near-duplicate of a proven format outperforms a wholly new one because familiarity does the work of removing risk while a small novel element supplies the reason to click — roughly a 90/10 split of template to twist.
Source: Alan Garnett
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

WHERE ON THE EXPOSURE CURVE is this format for this audience? Gannett already holds the reconciling pattern (115f4acc5069): liking follows an inverted-U against exposure count, rising with repetition to a peak and falling after, so a format has a finite number of uses. Both claims are true, on opposite sides of the peak — which converts an argument into a measurement problem: what is the instalment count, and is per-instalment performance still rising? Our mined-format table is weakly consistent with the decay side and worth watching rather than citing: the highest observed lifts sit on small match counts (I Built My Own After Getting Screwed, n=4, 2.92x; Exposing N Secrets, n=3, 2.76x) while the largest cohort in the table (Product Full Review, n=16) sits at 1.67x. That is confounded by naming granularity and cannot carry weight yet, but the store should record instalment index alongside every format so the peak becomes observable rather than argued about.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Contradicted: Corpus (33 channels, 831 videos): near-duplicates median 0.980x vs unique 1.005x (MWU z=-1.68, p=0.093). Age-adjusted the gap widens against repetition: 0.954x vs 1.016x (n=278 vs 534, z=-2.67, p=0.0076). Only 15 of 33 channels had repeats beating uniques. Our channels on first-28d views: repeated 0.99x (n=18) vs unique 1.00x (n=101), p=0.95. Conditional test, strict format frames (signature carrying >=2 literal frame words): 9 pairs where the prior instance scored >=1.5x produced follow-ups with median 1.01x and 0 of 9 reaching 1.5x (base rate 7%); median ratio next/prev = 0.29. Our channels: 3 such pairs, next median 0.72x, ratio 0.45, 0 of 3 reaching 1.5x.

Caveat: Signature repetition is a proxy for 'near-duplicate of a proven format' and catches generic title habits as well as deliberate franchises; a creator could execute the 90/10 rule without the title showing it. The conditional test that isolates deliberate repeats-of-a-hit is the strongest evidence but rests on only 12 pairs. Regression to the mean guarantees some decline from a >=1.5x instance regardless of format logic — but the claim asserts near-duplicates beat wholly new videos, and they do not beat them even before conditioning on a prior hit.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Supported: By 30s only 8 of 119 videos had lost 30%; by 60s 100 of 119 had; by 120s 117 of 119 had. Median retention: 77.5% at 30s, 61.6% at 60s, 54.1% at 120s. So the 30% threshold is crossed inside the 30-60s window for the large majority. Per channel at 60s: Channel C 30/30, Channel D 30/30, Channel F 10/10, Channel G 10/10, Channel E 6/9, Channel A 14/30. Median loss by window confirms the shape: 0-15s loses 6.5-9.4%, 15-30s loses 0-19.1%, 30-60s loses 9.7-24.9%.

Caveat: Channel A (Roblox gaming, 19-min median) is a genuine partial exception — fewer than half its videos cross 30% loss by 60s, and it needs ~120s. Channel E (52-min median) loses almost nothing between 15s and 30s (0.0% median) but then drops 24.9% in the 30-60s band, so the window shifts with runtime. The claim's diagnostic prescription is sound; the word 'always' is not.

Disputed

Signed off as a Law, but our own measurements disagree: it held in only 7% of readings across 18 channels.

Settle it by answering: Is the test measuring what the claim actually asserts, or does the claim hold under conditions the test does not capture?

Where the claim came from
Go back and do it again at the spot where you lost the first 30% of your viewers. It's usually in the first 30 to 60s of the video. Figure out what triggered this drop so you can see how to adjust based on the data.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Supported: rho(28d views, APV) is negative in 6/6 channels: Channel C -0.47, Channel D -0.46, Channel E -0.73, Channel A -0.49, Channel F -0.83, Channel G -0.61. Pooled -0.54 (n=119). Controlling duration barely moves it (pooled -0.51; per-channel -0.42 to -0.84). The top-view video sits below its channel's mean APV in 6/6 channels (e.g. Channel C 24.8% vs mean 46.7%; Channel A 21.9% vs 41.4%). Top-3-by-views median APV vs bottom-3: Channel C 29.7% vs 46.7%, Channel A 26.5% vs 45.7%, Channel E 25.7% vs 37.2%.

Caveat: This is CORRELATION only. We observe that high-view videos hold less; we cannot observe WHY. The stated mechanism (wider reach imports less-sticky viewers) is untested — a rival explanation fits the same data: high-view videos here are also longer (pooled rho views~duration +0.23, duration~APV -0.30), and broad-appeal topics may simply be structurally looser. Controlling duration leaves the effect nearly intact, which weakens but does not eliminate that rival. The repackaging half of the claim is untestable: we hold no before/after repackage events.

there is a correlation to the retention of that video lowering overall because you're getting new audience members with different viewing habits that are new to your channel that might not be as sticky. They might not want to watch for as long.

Contested — what would settle it

Is the video's retention high in ABSOLUTE terms, or high as a RESIDUAL — above what the channel's own retention-versus-views relationship predicts at that view count? Only the residual carries information; the absolute number is confounded by exactly the mechanism claim B names. OUR DATA SETTLES THIS: rank correlation between retention-at-50% and first-28d views is -0.45 (Channel C), -0.51 (Channel D), -0.85 (Channel E), -0.47 (Channel A), -0.89 (Channel F), +0.07 (Channel G) — negative on 5 of 6 channels, strongly so on the two small-n maker channels. The repackaging rule must therefore be re-specified as 'retention above the channel's fitted expectation at that view count', and the existing verdict table in our own pipeline should be checked against this.

Consistency of cadence matters more than the cadence itself. Whatever the interval, holding it reliably programs the audience to expect the next video; an erratic schedule costs more than a slow one. When you stack a new upload within about a day and a half of your previous one, that burst video tends to get roughly 25% fewer age-adjusted views than your typical non-burst upload — a pattern that held across 8 separate channels.
Source: the probe battery
Evidence and caveats →
Measurement record

Tested as: On this channel, do uploads that arrived in a daily burst (within ~1.5 days of the previous upload) underperform the channel's non-burst baseline? → Median age-normalised views for 9 uploads arriving within 1.5 days of the previous upload, minus the same for 216 non-burst uploads. (the claim predicts this goes down)

The question put to the data: On this channel, do uploads that arrived in a daily burst (within ~1.5 days of the previous upload) underperform the channel's non-burst baseline?

Exact arithmetic: Median age-normalised views for 10 uploads arriving within 1.5 days of the previous upload, minus the same for 221 non-burst uploads.

Each dot is one channel. Filled green held in the direction the claim predicts; hollow red did not. The dashed line is the threshold — an effect smaller than that is real in direction but too small to build a decision on. Signed toward the claim, so positive always means the claim’s own prediction showed up.
